question_text: A 2-year-old girl presents to the emergency department with a 3-minute episode of a tonic-clonic seizure. The patient carries a pink birthmark on the right side of her face extending from the forehead to the zygomatic arch. Which of the following findings is most likely on a head CT of this patient?

### Enhanced Information Summary

The patient, a 2-year-old girl, presents with a tonic-clonic seizure and a notable pink birthmark on the right side of her face, extending from the forehead to the zygomatic arch. This birthmark, known as a port-wine stain, is characteristic of Sturge-Weber syndrome (SWS), a neurocutaneous disorder. SWS is associated with leptomeningeal angiomas, which can affect the brain.

In cases of Sturge-Weber syndrome, neuroimaging, particularly a head CT, often reveals intraparenchymal abnormalities. One of the hallmark findings in SWS on CT scans is prominent intraparenchymal white matter calcification. This calcification results from the abnormal blood vessels associated with the leptomeningeal angiomas, which can lead to local ischemia and subsequent calcification.

The reasoning chains provided consistently link the facial port-wine stain to a likely diagnosis of Sturge-Weber syndrome and associate this condition with prominent intraparenchymal white matter calcification on a head CT. This aligns well with medical consensus on the neuroimaging findings in Sturge-Weber syndrome.

The retrieved evidence paths, while broad, support the association of neurocutaneous syndromes (like Sturge-Weber) with specific brain abnormalities, although they do not directly mention calcifications. However, the clinical presentation and the characteristic port-wine stain strongly suggest Sturge-Weber syndrome, making prominent intraparenchymal white matter calcification the most likely finding on a head CT in this scenario.
